doc.title: Norris Turney interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997

title: Life on the road: buses, segregated lodging, first white hotel
summary: Bus travel, staying in private homes across the tracks, and the first white hotel he stayed in, in Atlanta with Ray Charles in 1967.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: What was life like on the road in those days? Was it mostly bus travel first of all?
Yeah, bus. Sometimes we took the train.
What about accommodations at that time?

The accommodations were terrible you know. We couldn’t stay in hotels then. We had to go across the tracks and stay at people’s houses. As a matter of fact the first hotel I stayed in, a white hotel, was in Atlanta, Georgia, I was playing with Ray Charles. And they had just opened it up, that’s why we stayed there.
Well when you would get to a town with let’s say Billy Eckstine, was someone in the group responsible for going to the other side of the tracks and trying to find —
Yeah, it was somebody who was there, who lived there, would put us in different people’s homes.
Oh. So they knew you were coming.
And they’d come down and they made a few dollars off of that because you had to pay, or someone in the orchestra had to pay for putting you up.
Yeah but we paid for our own accommodations in those days. We paid for our own.
